note: 0074 named the residual cell of Nestor#17 and deliberately left it open: server-side ed25519 (shipped in 6ca5a5e) closed the cross-instance forgery cell, but the SIGNING instance still holds every one of its verifiers' private keys, so its operator can forge as anyone whose key lives there. Closing that fully means signing where the key lives -- a browser doing WebCrypto ed25519, or a client-side agent -- which is a UI build 0074 correctly refused to bundle into the crypto swap. This decision covers the half of that work that is server-side and can ship without the browser page: the SEAM that accepts a signature a client already produced and only verifies it, never signs it. `memory.add_pair(..., seal_sig=)` is the new parameter; `signing._message` is pinned as the wire contract a client signer must reproduce; the browser page that would actually hold a private key and call WebCrypto is explicitly NOT part of this and remains open, same as 0074 left it.

decisions.question: Given a client-produced signature, does the server VERIFY it or does it still need some notion of signing?
decisions.commitment: Verify only. `memory.add_pair(..., seal_sig=...)` never calls `signing.sign_seal` on this path -- it calls `signing.seal_is_valid` against the caller's own key, exactly the check a peer instance already makes on `portable.import_bundle`. `Keyring.signing_entry`'s refusal for an ed25519 entry holding only the public half is untouched; this path simply never reaches it, because nothing here needs to sign.
decisions.why: The whole point of the residual cell is that this instance must not need the private key to seal for a given verifier. A design that still routed a client signature through some signing call -- even a no-op one, even to 're-derive' or 'normalize' it -- would either require the private key again (defeating the point) or be a verify-in-signing's-clothing, which is a worse name for the same operation. Verify-only is also the smaller change: `signing.seal_is_valid` already existed and is exactly the function `portable.import_bundle` uses to accept a peer's seal, so this reuses a path that was already exercised by the two-instance tests in `test_asymmetric_seals.py` rather than inventing a second verification code path that could drift from the first.

decisions.question: `signing._message` was an internal detail -- both ends of every signature were produced inside this module. Does accepting an external signature change what it needs to be?
decisions.commitment: Yes: it becomes a FROZEN wire contract, documented as such in its own docstring and the module docstring, with the exact encoding pinned -- JSON array, field order `[source_norm, target_text, verifier]`, `separators=(",", ":")`, `ensure_ascii=False`, UTF-8 bytes. Not changed, only named for what it now is.
decisions.why: Every prior signature, HMAC or ed25519, was produced and checked by the same function in the same process, so any two calls agreed with each other by construction -- the encoding was free to change because nothing outside this module depended on its exact shape. A client signer breaks that invariant: it reproduces these bytes independently, without importing `nestor.signing`, so the two sides only agree if the encoding is pinned and never silently adjusted (a reordered field, an added separator space, an `ensure_ascii` flip) would desync every external signer from every server checking its signatures, and would do so silently -- signatures would simply stop verifying, with no exception pointing at the cause. `tests/test_client_signed_seals.py::TestMessageWireContractIsFrozen` pins the exact byte output for known inputs, including a non-ASCII case, with the expected bytes hardcoded rather than recomputed via `json.dumps` -- recomputing would make the pin true by construction and catch nothing (the house rule: mirror, do not import, when pinning a constant).

decisions.question: A supplied `seal_sig` does not verify. Refuse the whole call, or fall back to auto-signing as if none was supplied?
decisions.commitment: Refuse -- `InvalidSealSignatureError`, raised before `store.memory_find`/`memory_insert`/`memory_seal` ever run, so nothing is written: no sealed row, no draft, no row at all.
decisions.why: Falling back to auto-sign would mean a caller who tried to supply a signature and got it wrong (or had it tampered with in transit) ends up with the SERVER quietly signing on their behalf instead -- which only works at all when the server holds the private key, defeating the reason `seal_sig` exists for a public-only verifier, and for a private-half verifier it silently discards a verification failure that the caller had every reason to expect would be checked. The load-bearing property is that an UNVERIFIED signature must never reach the store as `status="sealed"` -- the Nestor#2 forgery one call deeper, this time via a signature nobody actually checked rather than a bare `status` column. Refusing before the write is the same discipline `_ledger_preflight` already applies for an unwritable ledger and `RejectedPairError`/`ConflictingSealError` already apply for a contested seal: every existing refusal in `add_pair` fires before the store is touched, and this one follows the same shape. Pinned by `tests/test_client_signed_seals.py::TestInvalidProvidedSignatureRefusesAndWritesNothing`, which asserts `store.memory_find(...)` is `None` after each refusal -- not just that an exception was raised, which a caller could otherwise ignore. One honest boundary, named by the audit rather than left implicit: this refusal holds exactly where verification is in force -- a keyring, or a shared `NESTOR_SEAL_KEY`. With signing fully OFF (no keyring, no key), `seal_is_valid` returns `True` for anything, as it does for every stored seal, so a supplied `seal_sig` is not checked either -- but that deployment already trusts any `status="sealed"` row by construction and warns that it does, so the client-signing seam grants no capability there that a bare `status` column did not already. The property is 'an unverified signature never lands sealed WHERE SIGNATURES ARE VERIFIED AT ALL', which is the only place the claim can mean anything.

decisions.question: Does supplying `seal_sig` change anything for a verifier who is NOT public-only -- private-half ed25519, hmac, or the shared `NESTOR_SEAL_KEY`?
decisions.commitment: Only if they choose to use it -- and then the same verify-only rule applies uniformly, with no special case for a caller who could have auto-signed instead. Omitting `seal_sig` (the default) is byte-for-byte the pre-existing behavior for every verifier kind; nothing about the auto-sign path was touched.
decisions.why: A per-kind carve-out (auto-sign unless the verifier is public-only) would mean the server sometimes has to know, ahead of the call, whether it CAN sign for a given name in order to decide whether to honor a supplied signature -- adding a branch to a security check for no safety benefit, since verifying a correct signature is always safe regardless of whether the server could have produced one itself. Uniformity is also what keeps `tests/test_client_signed_seals.py::TestAutoSignPathUnchanged` meaningful as a guard: it passes before AND after this change for the private-half/hmac/shared-key cases specifically because `seal_sig` defaulting to empty is a no-op for them, not because those cases were special-cased around.

decisions.question: Does this decision also ship the browser/agent page that would hold the private key and call WebCrypto?
decisions.commitment: No, deliberately, exactly as 0074 already decided for the crypto swap itself. This PR ships the seam (`memory.add_pair(seal_sig=)`, the frozen `_message` contract, `nestor.ui`'s `/api/seal`, `/api/seal-draft` and `/api/queue/seal` accepting the field) and nothing that produces a client signature.
decisions.why: The browser flow is real UI-architecture work with its own consequences -- key generation and storage in the browser, a signing UX, an enrollment story for handing a verifier's public key to the server -- and bundling it into this PR would repeat exactly the coupling 0074 named and declined for the ed25519 crypto swap: holding a server-side, independently testable improvement hostage to a browser rewrite. The seam is complete and provable on its own terms (`tests/test_client_signed_seals.py` proves a public-only verifier can now seal, given ANY correctly-signed message over the frozen contract -- a raw `cryptography` keypair standing in for whatever the eventual browser page produces, exercising the actual interface a real client will use without requiring that client to exist yet). The residual cell this leaves is stated openly here and in QUESTIONS.md §6, not implied to be closed.
